prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across the five frames on an outdoor asphalt court bordered by trees on the left and distant buildings (~30–50 m ahead), the depth map separates foreground structures from the receding ground plane and blacked-out sky. In Frames 1 and 2, as the camera wearer approaches the hoop on the upper left, its distance decreases from ~3–4 m to ~1.5–2.5 m (with the support pole partly out of view at the bottom-left), while a shirtless person stands ~6–10 m away on the lower-left court facing and looking toward the wearer, positioned ~4–5 m behind a mid-air basketball (~2.5–3 m away in Frame 2). In Frame 3, the wearer turns right and tilts down toward the open court so the hoop and person leave the view, leaving only the asphalt gradient and the basketball partly visible at the bottom-right within arm's reach (<1 m). In Frame 4, the wearer faces the hoop closely (~0.5–1 m on the left) and extends their right arm and hand within arm's reach (~0.3–0.5 m on the right) to hold the ball above the rim (partially occluding the sky), before passing beneath the hoop in Frame 5 where only the backboard corner remains at the top-left (~1–1.5 m) and the person reappears ~8–10 m away on the lower-right facing the wearer. Depth clarifies that the airborne ball in Frame 2 is several metres closer than the person behind it and captures the fine 3D mesh of the net in Frame 4, which are harder to gauge in RGB alone, though per-frame contrast normalization makes the <1 m arm, ball, and hoop in Frame 4 appear dimmer (mid-grey) than the Frame 2 backboard, and the transparent backboard is rendered as an opaque flat plane with bleeding edges along the Frame 1 pole.
descriptions.segmentation: Against the black background of the outdoor court scene, the segmentation map isolates discrete foreground and background instances as the camera wearer approaches the hoop (Frames 1–2), turns toward the open court (Frame 3), reaches up with the ball at the rim (Frame 4), and moves past the hoop (Frame 5). It tracks the shirtless person standing ~6–10 m away (facing and looking toward the wearer with nothing within arm's reach) at the bottom-left in Frames 1–2 (partly clipped by the bottom frame edge in Frame 1) and at the bottom-right in Frame 5, while locating the airborne `sports ball` (~2.5–3 m away in Frame 2) in front of and ~4–5 m closer than the standing person. The map also detects tiny distant `person` instances (~30–40 m away near the background playground and tree line, ~20–30 m behind the nearer person) to the right in Frames 1, 2, 3, and 5 (with the rightmost instance in Frame 5 partly cut off at the frame border), which are only a few pixels tall and very hard to spot in the RGB strip alone. However, the segmentation is highly unreliable for major nearby objects: in Frame 1 it merges and mislabels the basketball hoop (~3–4 m above on the left) and ball as an `airplane`, and in Frame 2 it misclassifies the cropped hoop pole at the bottom-left edge (~1.5 m away) as a `person`. Furthermore, it completely fails to segment the hoop in Frames 2, 4, and 5, as well as the basketball and the wearer's raised right arm and hand within arm's reach (<1 m) in Frames 3 and 4.
descriptions.pose: Across the five-frame sequence on the outdoor basketball court, the pose map detects a single yellow body skeleton only in Frame 1 and remains completely blank in Frames 2 through 5, with no magenta hand skeletons present in any frame. In Frame 1, the skeleton is located in the lower-left at ~8–10 m from the camera wearer (roughly 5 m behind and below the basketball hoop on the left), showing the shirtless person standing upright with torso and head facing toward the camera wearer, arms angled down near the hips (nothing within arm's reach), and lower legs slightly clipped at the bottom border. Even though the person is small and shadowed in the wide-angle RGB image, these joint keypoints clearly resolve their frontal body orientation, hip alignment, and slight knee bend. However, the pose estimation is completely unreliable across the rest of the sequence as the wearer approaches the hoop, turns away, jumps to shoot, and lands. It fails to detect the same standing person at ~6–10 m in Frames 2 and 5, misses all distant background figures (~30–40 m away), and completely omits the camera wearer's own unoccluded right arm and hand holding the basketball within arm's reach (~0.3–0.5 m) in Frame 4.
